title: Content-Based and Content-Neutral Laws
short: Laws that regulate speech because of its subject or message are content-based and get strict scrutiny (Reed v. Town of Gilbert, 2015); content-neutral laws get intermediate scrutiny; viewpoint discrimination is the most suspect of all.
trouble: Students think a law that treats all viewpoints equally is content-neutral. A law can be viewpoint-neutral yet content-based if it singles out a subject (all political signs, for example).

blocks.html: Note: This is an educational course, not legal advice.

After Brandenburg, the next question in most speech cases is: what is the law regulating? The Court's central distinction is between laws that target speech because of what it says and laws that regulate speech for other reasons. It borrows the tiers from Con Law I: heightened scrutiny.

head: Kind of law
Example
Review
rows: a ban on signs criticizing the mayor, but not praising
Content-based: depends on the subject or message
a ban on all political signs, or a code with different rules for "ideological" and "directional" signs
strict scrutiny: compelling interest, narrowly tailored
no signs larger than 16 square feet; no loudspeakers after 10 p.m.

opts.facts: Gilbert, Arizona, had a sign code with different size and time limits for "ideological," "political" and "temporary directional" signs. A small church that announced its services with temporary directional signs found them far more restricted than political or ideological signs.
opts.reasoning: Justice Thomas wrote that a law is content-based on its face if it applies to particular speech because of the topic discussed or the idea or message expressed, whatever the government's motive. The sign code's categories depended on what the signs said, so strict scrutiny applied, and the code failed it.

blocks.html: Why treat content so strictly? Because laws that pick out messages let government shape public debate, the very danger the First Amendment exists to prevent. Viewpoint discrimination is worse still: in Rosenberger v. Rector and Visitors of the University of Virginia (1995) a university could not deny printing funds to a student paper because of its religious viewpoint, and in Matal v. Tam (2017) the government could not refuse to register trademarks that "disparage" people, since giving offense is itself a viewpoint. Some justices have worried that Reed's approach sweeps in many ordinary rules, such as rules about where signs may stand; the Court has said that rules based on location, not topic, are content-neutral.

blocks.name: cv-scrutiny
blocks.cap: Speech regulated because of its content: strict scrutiny.

blocks.html: Content-based laws (by subject or message) get strict scrutiny (Reed v. Town of Gilbert (2015)); viewpoint discrimination is the most suspect of all; content-neutral laws get intermediate scrutiny.

blocks.title: Neutral as to viewpoint, but not content
blocks.q: A city bans all signs about elections on public sidewalks, for every party and candidate. Content-neutral?
steps: But whether a sign is banned depends on its subject: elections.
Under Reed that is content-based, so strict scrutiny applies.
blocks.a: No; it is content-based (though viewpoint-neutral) and gets strict scrutiny.

blocks.title: Sort the law
blocks.q: A county forbids any amplified sound in parks after 9 p.m. What kind of law?
steps: It applies to all amplified sound, whatever is said.
It is content-neutral, so intermediate scrutiny applies under the time, place and manner test.

blocks.html: Thinking a law that treats all viewpoints equally is content-neutral. A law can be viewpoint-neutral yet content-based if it singles out a subject (all political signs, for example). Check: would you have to read the sign to know whether the law applies? If so, it is content-based.

cards.text: No signs criticizing the city council
No trademark registration for disparaging marks
cards.why: Matal v. Tam: giving offense is a viewpoint.
